Microsoft has agreed to spend billions of dollars on Mistral’s computing infrastructure in Europe under a deal that will also expand distribution of the French ⁠AI startup’s technology through the U.S. cloud and software giant, the companies said on Tuesday.

headline: Space Exploration Day | How are astronauts trained?
body: If you want to be in space, you’ll need training. A lot of it. Here’s a look at all the different training — from spacewalk to simulation — that astronauts undergo to be efficient and valiant when, after much waiting, they finally get to space!
full_body:

Today's Cache Your download of the top 5 technology stories of the day.

By way of our sharp fascination towards a spaceflight event when it happens, we tend to forget reading into the entire process that led to that moment. Process, in today’s ‘all-instant’ era, seems to lose value unless you are part of it. Going to space in a rocket and coming back sounds simply doable but an astronaut undergoes rigorous training for years just to be physically and mentally capable of doing it. All the complex processes involved in this preparation are what is referred to as ‘Astronaut training’.

Aside from physical training, medical tests, etc. much of these processes involve simulating conditions that an astronaut would encounter in their trip to space.

The term ‘extra-vehicular activity’ means any activity that an astronaut performs in outer space outside of the spacecraft in which they have come. Say, you are exploring a planet or taking a spacewalk outside your spacecraft. This is EVA. Training for this involves submerging into a neutral buoyancy pool where astronauts wear specially designed suits that simulate microgravity. In this training, astronauts learn how to use EVA tools, communicate with EVA crewmates, and develop sharp and full situational awareness. EVA training for ISS often takes place at NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) at the Johnson Space Center, Houston, U.S. and at Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center, in Russia.

Suppose you are an astronaut tasked to go and explore Mars. How can you go without understanding what the Mars environment is like and how can you scientifically explore without knowing what to look for? Geology and field training helps astronauts with both these. This training includes practice in environments similar to the one that they will go to and teaches them how to look for, collect, and analyse samples. For this, places on Earth with similar geological features such as trenches, volcanic regions, craters, etc. are chosen as training grounds.

Before the Apollo mission, the astronauts came to Hawaii to train on the Big Island’s lunar landscapes. They rode moon buggy vehicles, collected soil samples as if they were on the moon.

Anything can happen when you are travelling to, in, and coming back from space. All of those survival-type space films are just an extension of this idea.

headline: What goals does Semicon 2.0 aim to achieve? | Explained
body: What are the key focus areas of Semicon 2.0? How is it different from the first phase? Why is India focusing on semiconductor manufacturing? What incentives does the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme offer?
full_body:

O n July 15, the Union Cabinet cleared the second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), and the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS), with a ₹1.27 lakh crore and ₹62,500 crore outlay, respectively. The programmes are aimed at encouraging the next cohort of semiconductor fabrication, assembly, and packaging facilities in India, as well as following through on encouraging more phone assembly and component manufacturing in the country. The government expects the scheme to draw ₹4 lakh crore in investment, ₹2 lakh crore in production, and ₹1 lakh crore in exports over its tenure of five years.

ISM’s first phase was approved in December 2021 with an outlay of ₹76,000 crore. Following an amendment in 2022, the programme was empowered to provide for up to 50% capital subsidy for big-ticket projects, such as Micron’s memory chip packaging facility in Sanand, Gujarat. The funds were also directed to the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, which was designed to incentivise additional manufacturing of smaller electronics components.

The Gazette notification laying out the precise details of the second phase is set to be published by next month. In the meantime, Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) Additional Secretary Amitesh Kumar Sinha have offered a few details of the expanded scope of the programme.

The main change is that the ISM programme will now cover a larger part of the electronics manufacturing ecosystem, including areas that were partially addressed in the previous phase. These include encouraging chip design talent, capital machinery (the large equipment used in chip-making facilities), chemicals and gases that are of semiconductor-grade purity, and research and development efforts.

The newer scheme will also trim capital subsidies to 30-40%, Mr. Sinha said, as the semiconductor industry is likely to get more attractive in India even with less incentives. The government is also less likely to offer land support, as State governments have shown increasing enthusiasm for hosting such projects by providing land at token prices and offering their own incentives on top of those provided by the Union government.

Of the 12 manufacturing and packaging units approved in phase 1, with a total committed investment of ₹1.64 lakh crore, most are semiconductor packaging units. Nine such units are spread across Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Assam, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh. In addition, there is a silicon fabrication unit, and one gallium-nitride Micro LED display fabrication unit. The Tata Electronics fab is set to start commercial production in 2028.

full_body:
India’s first hydrogen-powered train is ready for launch! Marking a major milestone for Indian Railways, the country’s first hydrogen will be flagged off by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on July 17. This is the first time that India is introducing a train that produces its own electricity onboard using hydrogen, which is widely regarded as the cleanest fuel available. This also places India among the few countries in the world that are testing hydrogen trains. Why is India’s first hydrogen train project important? What route will the train run on and at what speeds? We take a look at 10 important facts about India’s first hydrogen train that you shouldn’t miss:

Indian Railways’ first hydrogen train will run between Jind and Sonipat in Haryana. On the 89 kilometres route the train will stop at Pandu Pindara Junction, Lalit Khera Halt, Bhambhewa, Isapur Kheri Halt, Butane Halt, Khandrai Halt, Rabrah Halt, Lath Halt, Mohana, Barwasni Halt.

India’s first hydrogen first powered train is designed for speeds of up to 110 kilometres per hour. The train will run at a maximum operational speed of 75 kilometres per hour.

The Hydrogen train generates power by combining hydrogen with oxygen to produce electricity. The resultant by-product is only water vapour. It is a near-zero emissions operation, making it one of the cleanest fuel options available. This marks a milestone for Indian Railways in green mobility.

The hydrogen-powered train has two hydrogen driving power cars and eight trailer coaches. Each driving power car has hydrogen fuel cells, lithium iron phosphate batteries and hydrogen storage cylinders, which operate together to generate traction power. Positioned at either end of the train, the two driving power cars each generate 1,200 kW (1,600 hp), providing a combined output sufficient to propel the entire train at speeds of up to 110 kmph.

Where will the hydrogen train be refueled? Like petrol and CNG-powered vehicles require dedicated filling stations, the hydrogen train also needs specialised refuelling infrastructure. To support its operations, Indian Railways has set up the country's largest hydrogen refuelling facility for the railway network at Jind in Haryana.

The hydrogen-fueled train has been designed, engineered and integrated in India using indigenous technology, highlighting the country's expanding capabilities in advanced railway engineering. RDSO prepared the technical specifications and led the design approval process, while Medha Servo Drives integrated the trainset. The Integral Coach Factory was responsible for the train's exterior.

To ensure safe operations, a comprehensive, multi-layered safety architecture has been designed to detect hydrogen leaks, excessive heat, flames and smoke. This corridor has been chosen to demonstrate the safety, reliability and operational feasibility of hydrogen-powered passenger services under normal operating conditions.
